claim: Preschoolers (mean 54 months) rarely run the variable-isolating test when evidence is unambiguous (1/20, 5%) and do so about half the time when it is ambiguous (9/20 = 45% and 10/20 = 50%). About half of the ambiguous group still does not. Gap search 2026-10-27: no replication or failed replication found among 112 Europe PMC citing records; conceptual extensions exist (see K26, K27).
agent_test: Same-lab, 2 experiments only (N=60, N=40). Build a toy rule task where one rule dominates vs two rules tie; count how often the agent runs the one splitting test at equal tokens. Expect a shift in rate, not all-or-none.

claim: Given only a stuck pair (Experiment 2), children invented a new splitting intervention (stand the pair on end), 9/20 vs 1/20. Same lab and same effect size, so not an independent replication.
agent_test: Give the agent a task whose only informative test is not on its menu; measure whether S7 proposes a new test when rules tie and not when they do not.

claim: Ambiguity does not raise the breadth of play (mean about 3.8-4.1 action categories across conditions). Only the one critical action rose (63% vs 18%). The response is selective, not wild.
agent_test: Score S3 output by whether candidates split the live hypotheses, not by count. Compare breadth and split rate across a tie condition and a no-tie condition.

claim: Children play more with a confounded item and go back to it over a novel one (Schulz & Bonawitz 2007, N=64; Gweon & Schulz 2008, N=32). All papers come from one lab family.
agent_test: Open-mode rule: resolve a live tie before moving to a new item. Compare with a novelty-first control at equal tokens.

claim: Exploration effort scales with how hard two hypotheses are to tell apart (16 contrasts, model-vs-play r=0.95 across condition means). Box content did not predict play. Participant count is inconsistent inside the paper (160 in abstract; 184 recruited minus 16 excluded in methods).
agent_test: Set the number of probes from output distance between rival rules; test against a fixed budget at equal tokens.

claim: Ambiguity is relative to a held theory. Children with a theory explore more when evidence contradicts it; children with no theory prefer novelty regardless (95 + 31 children, interaction F(1,59)=6.02). A second lab (van Schijndel 2015, shadow-size domain) reports all children who saw theory-violating evidence ran an unconfounded informative test at the start of play vs about half after confirming evidence (abstract only, not opened).
agent_test: Compare S7 with and without a written working rule at S2. The no-rule agent should show no surprise-driven test.

claim: Teaching or an ostensive demonstration of one function narrows exploration (play 119 s vs 206 s baseline; action kinds 4.0 vs 6.15), also when the teaching was overheard and meant for a similar learner.
agent_test: Run open-mode S3 with and without a worked example in context; count distinct candidate classes. All three lines are one paper.

claim: Children not told the hypothesis space gathered enough data to settle the rule only 32% of the time, versus 71% when told (N=85, p=0.002). They also stopped early and repeated tests.
agent_test: Compare an agent given a short live-hypothesis list at S2 against one asked to explore unprompted; measure the share of runs where the data settle the rule.

claim: In a closed rule set, ideal information-gain policies take fewer steps and always collect enough data. Children take more steps and often stop short. A pure info-gain objective is not child-like.
agent_test: Exact EIG over an enumerated rule set in code should beat the model's own choice; test at equal tokens.

claim: Plain LLMs choose informative tests poorly in interactive tasks: GPT-3 shows no directed exploration on the horizon task; blicket LMs eliminate hypotheses slower than an info-gain oracle (some worse than random); most LLMs underperform humans in Little Alchemy 2; GPT-3.5/4 fail bandit exploration.
agent_test: Compare model-chosen tests with code-chosen max-EIG tests on a closed rule set; count steps to one live rule.

claim: LLMs show a disjunctive bias: they find OR machines far better than AND machines across model families, sizes and prompt styles (default, ReAct, Reflexion, CoT). Adults show the same bias under passive evidence; 4-year-olds do not. LaMDA was also weakest in causal reasoning.
agent_test: Force low-prior rules into the candidate set; compare AND-rule accuracy with and without forcing.

claim: Sampling many distinct hypotheses as code and then choosing actions that eliminate the most removes the AND/OR gap (figures only). A related method (rule proposal, Monte Carlo update, info-gain test choice) beat a ReAct agent on Zendo (6.55/8 vs 4.60/8). A typed-state-machine scaffold helped on blicket with rule change. Size of the gain, new numbers: Zendo experiment choice by code-computed InfoGain 6.55/8 vs LLM-chosen 4.72/8 vs random 5.84/8 (GPT-4 Turbo class, calls not tokens). GX-Chen exploration progress is near random at 4 objects (0.968) and noisy at 8; no Q&A table value found. Alderete: scaffold beat the context-graph arm (89.1% vs 77.3%, p=0.015) but Base was 87.3%. Not tested at equal tokens or modern scale.
agent_test: Implement enumerate-then-eliminate on a blicket-like task; compare with a ReAct baseline at equal tokens. Read the GX-Chen values from the figures before relying on them.

claim: Test quality tracks success: information gathered (rho about 0.76, read from a figure) and the share of tests that could contradict the leading rule (rho 0.65-0.74, from a figure) both go with success. Longer replies and early exit go with failure.
agent_test: Log per-test info gain and incompatible-test share in our loop; check correlation with final accuracy.

claim: A prompt asking for the test that would break the leading rule (Think-in-Opposites) raised rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average across eleven LLMs on a 2-4-6 task. On blicket it helped thinking models (Qwen3-32B 0.57 to 0.86) but not non-thinking ones (0.64 to 0.56). Distilling it into Qwen3-32B reached 0.77 (CORRECTED: about 70% of the prompt gain). Table re-read: other thinking models gain only 0.02-0.11 (8B 0.32 to 0.40, 14B 0.50 to 0.61, R1-70B 0.41 to 0.43, QwQ 0.80 to 0.82); non-thinking is mixed (+0.08, -0.05, -0.08, +0.04). On Wason thinking-model tokens per turn rose 12-58% in four of five models (32B +41%), fell 17% in QwQ.
agent_test: Add a break-the-leading-rule step in S7 and compare, with a code check that the proposed test really splits the rules.

claim: Humans who plan tests but see outcomes from someone else's tests do worse than passive observers (conjunctive object ID: Active 0.69, Observer 0.45, Proposer 0.12; N=306). The benefit comes from seeing the result of your own test. Caveat: the Proposer saw outcomes of a different person's tests, so plan-outcome mismatch is not separated from lack of control. No LLM batch-vs-interleaved arm exists.
agent_test: Compare an interleaved run-test-then-choose loop with a batch plan of tests in one pass at equal tokens. Alternative reading: proposers saw outcomes mismatched to their own plans.

claim: Reasoning-trained models explore better than chat models in the same task (o1 177 elements vs GPT-4o 35 in Little Alchemy 2; gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner near top humans on OR). Results are mixed: o4-mini used few tests with modest AND accuracy, and the Pan paper contradicts itself on DeepSeek-R1: the abstract names only o1, the main text gives R1 85 vs humans 42 elements (t=3.40), and Appendix C.2 calls R1 near human-level and below o1 (checked in the full text).
agent_test: Compare reasoning-mode and chat-mode runs of the same scaffold at equal tokens on the same blicket set.

claim: Temperature does not raise useful exploration: temperature x uncertainty beta=2.911 but temperature x empowerment 0.196 (p=0.286). Models decide early on uncertainty and weigh empowerment late (SAE layers, one open model).
agent_test: Do not use temperature for diversity; compare with a code-kept list of directions already tried.

claim: In large open worlds, information gain describes human exploration less well than entropy or empowerment (child sample 26 in Crafter; Little Alchemy 2 regression). In small closed hypothesis sets info gain is the right selector. Two selectors for two modes.
agent_test: Use info gain at S7 (closed set) and a diversity or novelty-distance score at S3 (open set); compare against a single-selector variant.

claim: A code-side contradiction monitor on the confirmed model detects regime change (sensitivity 100% post-switch, PPV 90.5-100%). A typed state machine raised reasoning-eligible accuracy 73.3% to 93.9%, but gave no effect in the stochastic condition and lowered raw accuracy when used alone.
agent_test: Add a code contradiction signal that triggers re-testing; compare with a scheduled recheck. Caveats: one company, one model family, one-tailed tests, preprint.

claim: Passing a text vignette on causal or blicket items is weak evidence of exploration skill: GPT-3 got 12 of 12 vignettes correct or human-like yet showed no directed exploration live; LaMDA answers looked recalled (it cited the blicket papers).
agent_test: Judge S7 from live loops with renamed machines; track the vignette-vs-live gap as a metric.

claim: Models give the statistically nearest answer. In a tool-innovation task children (85.2%) and adults (95.7%) found the unrelated functional object, while LLMs matched association but missed innovation.
agent_test: Force a different reading of the object in open mode; compare novelty of candidates against plain re-sampling.

claim: Free exploration with no goal predicted faster later goal finding in a maze (coverage 22/44/71%, steps to goal 95/89/66). Preliminary workshop result.
agent_test: Short open-mode S3 before the task vs none, at equal total tokens.

claim: Forced random exploration steps before commitment beat imitation of expert policies for RL agents (Decision Transformer reward 0.16 to 2.06-2.37 with 5-15 forced steps).
agent_test: Force k untried actions before selection; compare with free selection.

claim: Good prediction does not imply good experiment choice: in BoxingGym all tested LLMs struggled at design and discovery; in DiscoveryWorld the best agent finished 38% of easy tasks vs 66% for humans, and a hypothesis-first agent found more explanation but finished fewer tasks.
agent_test: Use BoxingGym EIG regret as a benchmark for the S7 selector.

claim: No direct replication, failed replication, or LLM version of the Cook 2011 bead contrast was found. 112 Europe PMC citing records were scanned (2014-2026) and none is a direct replication; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited, so non-indexed work (OSF, proceedings) is unchecked.
agent_test: Run our own base-rate manipulation on the agent: same stuck-pair evidence, prior 'all work' vs 'half work'; measure the rate of the isolating test.

claim: Young children pick the variable-isolating action when it is placed on a menu (Lapidow and Walker 2020, ages 4-6, gears: clear preference for removing one gear, kept when the informative action was less likely to give a pleasing effect). This favours the reading that the low base rate of 5% in free play comes from not generating or not wanting the test, not from lacking it. Abstract only.
agent_test: Give the agent a menu of candidate tests with the splitting test on it vs no menu; compare the rate it picks the split.

claim: Recognising that evidence is confounded and choosing a controlled test are separate skills in 3-6-year-olds (Moeller 2022, N=57, unrelated; two-variable controlled choice on both trials 46%, on one 40%, on none 14%; chance chi2(2)=13.49, p=.001). Also Koksal 2021 (N=60, ages 5-6) shows detection by asking for more information (abstract only).
agent_test: Test whether the agent's own statement that it is unsure predicts running the split; compare with a code-computed tie.

claim: Siegel 2021 sample size: 184 recruited minus 16 excluded = 168 analysed (about 7 experiments of 24), not 160 as in the abstract. Exp 4-7 showed 75-85% of children exploring longer on harder contrasts.
agent_test: Use N=168 in all notes.

claim: MODEL ONLY, not an LLM measurement: a code gate (exact rule-list tie check) beats always-split when gate cost < (1 - tie rate) x split cost, and never-split beats an expensive gate when ties are rare. With split 300 tokens, gate 20: accuracy per 1k tokens at tie rate 0.1 is 19.8 (gate) vs 12.7 (never) vs 3.3 (always); with gate 150 it is 5.5 vs 12.7 vs 3.3. A model-judge gate with recall 0.5 reaches only 0.975 accuracy at tie rate 0.1 and 0.768 at 0.9.
agent_test: Measure real gate cost in tokens on the toy task and compare with the break-even; run all three policies at equal token budgets.

claim: Choosing experiments by code-computed information gain beat LLM-chosen experiments on Zendo by about 1.8 of 8 scenes (6.55 vs 4.72, GPT-4 Turbo class); a random proposer reranked by InfoGain did about as well as the LLM proposer. Batch inference plateaus after 15 hypotheses, online after 75. Compute counted as LLM calls, not tokens.
agent_test: Replicate with a modern model at equal tokens, comparing LLM-chosen, random-reranked and LLM-proposed-reranked tests.

claim: Open after gap search: no LLM study of (a) a stated hypothesis or worked example narrowing candidate tests (Bonawitz analogue, gap 8), (b) interleaved test-then-choose vs batch plan (gap 6), (c) a switch rule from information gain to entropy or empowerment (gap 10), or (d) training isolation first then repeating the Cook contrast (gap 4). Related abstracts only (Lee 2025, Xiong 2026, 2507.08210, Ruggeri 2019, Legare 2012).
agent_test: Four small toy runs, one per gap; each needs real model calls.
